steps.label: Do Now: Data Types (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Data Types (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a program check the data type when a value is stored, and not later?Show the answer

The wrong kind of value would cause problems in every line that uses it. Stopping at once shows exactly where it went in.

From 2.2: data types. The program stops with an error.

1  DECLARE Name : STRING
2  DECLARE Height : INTEGER
3  DECLARE Paid : BOOLEAN
4  Name <- "Nok"
5  Height <- 1.47
6  Paid <- TRUE
7  OUTPUT Name
Total: 2 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: the wrong data type

steps.text: This is a different program. Do the same steps with your program.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Town : STRING
DECLARE Lives : STRING
Town <- "Songkhla"
Lives <- 3
OUTPUT Town

steps.text: DECLARE does not store anything. It only gives each variable its data type.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Town : STRING
DECLARE Lives : STRING
Town <- "Songkhla"
Lives <- 3
OUTPUT Town

steps.text: Line 3 stores "Songkhla" in Town. It is in quotes, so it is text. Town is a STRING, so that is fine.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Town : STRING
DECLARE Lives : STRING
Town <- "Songkhla"
Lives <- 3
OUTPUT Town

steps.text: Line 4 stores 3 in Lives. 3 has no quotes: it is a whole number. Lives was declared as a STRING, so the program stops here, on line 4.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Town : STRING
DECLARE Lives : STRING
Town <- "Songkhla"
Lives <- 3
OUTPUT Town
Lives <- 3: stops here

steps.text: The fix goes on the DECLARE line. A whole number needs INTEGER, so line 2 becomes DECLARE Lives : INTEGER. Now do yours.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Town : STRING
DECLARE Lives : STRING
Town <- "Songkhla"
Lives <- 3
OUTPUT Town

steps.label: Do Now: DIV, MOD and a Constant (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: DIV, MOD and a Constant (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is the team size a constant and not a variable?Show the answer

It is set once and the program never needs to change it while it runs.

From 2.1 and 2.2. 30 is typed in.

1  CONSTANT TeamSize <- 4
2  DECLARE Pupils : INTEGER
3  INPUT Pupils
4  OUTPUT DIV(Pupils, TeamSize)
5  OUTPUT MOD(Pupils, TeamSize)
Total: 3 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: DIV, MOD and a constant

steps.text: This is a different program. 27 is typed in. Do the same steps with your program.
steps.visual:
CONSTANT BoxSize <- 6
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, BoxSize)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, BoxSize)

steps.text: BoxSize is a constant: it is 6 on every line that uses it.
steps.visual:
CONSTANT BoxSize <- 6
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, BoxSize)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, BoxSize)
BoxSize = 6

steps.text: DIV gives the whole number of times. 6 x 4 = 24, and 6 x 5 = 30 is too many.
steps.visual:
CONSTANT BoxSize <- 6
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, BoxSize)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, BoxSize)
DIV(27, 6) = 4

steps.text: MOD gives what is left over: 27 - 24 = 3.
steps.visual:
CONSTANT BoxSize <- 6
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, BoxSize)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, BoxSize)
MOD(27, 6) = 3

steps.text: Now line 1 is changed to 8. Every line that uses BoxSize uses 8 now. 8 x 3 = 24, so MOD(27, 8) is 27 - 24 = 3. Now do yours.
steps.visual:
CONSTANT BoxSize <- 8
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, BoxSize)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, BoxSize)

steps.label: 2.3: Conditional Statements
steps.content:
Programming, Logic and Testing

2.3: Conditional Statements

Year 8

  • Today: about 20 minutes of notes. Then use your notes in Data Bridge.
  • The big question: how does a program decide what to do, and how do we know it decides correctly?
Think → Pair → ShareA game says "Game over" when your lives run out. What does the game need to check, and how often?Show the answer

Collect ideas: it checks the number of lives, again and again. Today shows how a program asks a question like this and chooses what to do.

steps.label: IF, THEN and ELSE
steps.content:
IF, THEN and ELSE

1  DECLARE Age : INTEGER
2  INPUT Age
3  IF Age >= 13 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Join the club"
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT "Not yet"
7  ENDIF
  • Line 3 holds the condition: Age >= 13.
  • TRUE: the THEN branch runs (line 4).
  • FALSE: the ELSE branch runs (line 6).
  • 14 typed in: Join the club. 12 typed in: Not yet.
Condition: a question with only two answers, TRUE or FALSE.
Selection: an IF statement selects which branch (group of lines) runs. Only one branch runs.

WHY? A condition cannot be TRUE and FALSE at the same time, so the program never runs both branches.

Think → Pair → ShareA lift door opens when a button is pressed. Why does a program need a question with only two answers to decide this?Show the answer

Ideas: the button is pressed or it is not. Two answers means the program always knows exactly which lines to run.

steps.label: Your Notes: IF, THEN and ELSE
steps.content:
Your Notes: IF, THEN and ELSE

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

Condition
A question with only two answers: TRUE or FALSE. Example: Age >= 13.
Selection
An IF statement is a selection statement. TRUE: the THEN branch runs. FALSE: the ELSE branch runs.
WHY only one branch runs
A condition cannot be TRUE and FALSE at the same time.

steps.label: Six Comparison Operators
steps.content:
Six Comparison Operators

Comparison operator: a symbol that compares two values. The answer is TRUE or FALSE. Here Score is 10.
OperatorMeaningExampleAnswer
=is equal toScore = 10TRUE
<>is not equal toScore <> 10FALSE
<is less thanScore < 10FALSE
<=is less than or equal toScore <= 10TRUE
>is more thanScore > 10FALSE
>=is more than or equal toScore >= 10TRUE

WHY? Put the value into the condition first, then say the symbol in words: "10 is more than or equal to 10" is TRUE.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does = in a condition need a different symbol from the <- that stores a value?Show the answer

Ideas: <- changes a variable. = only asks a question and changes nothing.

steps.label: Your Notes: Comparison Operators
steps.content:
Your Notes: Comparison Operators

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

Comparison operator
A symbol that compares two values. The answer is TRUE or FALSE.
Copy the six operators
= equal to   <> not equal to   < less than
<= less than or equal to   > more than   >= more than or equal to
WHY say it in words
Put the value in, then read the symbol in words. Then you can see if it is TRUE or FALSE.

steps.label: Compare: > and >=
steps.content:
Compare: > and >=

The rule: pupils aged 13 or older can join the club. Two programmers wrote line 3 differently.

A: IF Age > 13 THEN

B: IF Age >= 13 THEN

13 > 13 is FALSE. 13 >= 13 is TRUE.
Age typed inA outputsB outputs
12Not yetNot yet
13Not yetJoin the club
14Join the clubJoin the club
Rule words: "or more" is >=. "more than" is >. "or less" is <=. "less than" and "under" are <.

WHY? Only 13, the number written in the condition, gives a different answer. B follows the rule.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy do 12 and 14 not show which program is wrong?Show the answer

Both programs give the same output for them. Only one value makes the two programs disagree.

steps.label: Your Notes: > and >=
steps.content:
Your Notes: > and >=

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

> and >=
> means more than: 13 > 13 is FALSE. >= means more than or equal to: 13 >= 13 is TRUE.
Rule words
"or more": >=. "more than": >. "or less": <=. "less than" or "under": <.
WHY check the number in the condition
It is the only value where > and >= give different answers.

steps.label: Three Outcomes: An IF Inside an IF
steps.content:
Three Outcomes: An IF Inside an IF

1  DECLARE Score : INTEGER
2  INPUT Score
3  IF Score >= 80 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Gold"
5  ELSE
6      IF Score >= 50 THEN
7          OUTPUT "Silver"
8      ELSE
9          OUTPUT "Bronze"
10      ENDIF
11  ENDIF
ScoreConditions checkedOutput
8585 >= 80 is TRUEGold
6565 >= 80 is FALSE, 65 >= 50 is TRUESilver
3030 >= 80 is FALSE, 30 >= 50 is FALSEBronze
  • Each IF needs its own ENDIF.
Nested IF: an IF inside the ELSE branch of another IF. It gives three outcomes.

WHY? One IF has only two branches. The second IF splits the ELSE branch into two more.

Think → Pair → ShareFor 85, why is line 6 never checked?Show the answer

Ideas: 85 >= 80 is TRUE, so the THEN branch runs and the whole ELSE branch is skipped.

steps.label: Your Notes: Nested IF
steps.content:
Your Notes: Nested IF

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

Nested IF
An IF inside the ELSE branch of another IF. It gives three outcomes, like Gold, Silver and Bronze.
How to trace it
Check the first IF. TRUE: its THEN branch runs and the whole ELSE is skipped. FALSE: go to the ELSE and check the second IF.
WHY each IF needs its own ENDIF
The computer must know where each IF ends.

steps.label: Compare: Which IF Comes First?
steps.content:
Compare: Which IF Comes First?

Same rule: 80 or more is Gold, 50 to 79 is Silver. The checks are in a different order. 85 is typed in.

A: 50 first. Output: Silver

DECLARE Score : INTEGER
INPUT Score
IF Score >= 50 THEN
    OUTPUT "Silver"
ELSE
    IF Score >= 80 THEN
        OUTPUT "Gold"
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Bronze"
    ENDIF
ENDIF

B: 80 first. Output: Gold

DECLARE Score : INTEGER
INPUT Score
IF Score >= 80 THEN
    OUTPUT "Gold"
ELSE
    IF Score >= 50 THEN
        OUTPUT "Silver"
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Bronze"
    ENDIF
ENDIF

WHY? Every score of 80 or more is also 50 or more. In A, the 50 check is TRUE first, so the Gold check is skipped. A can never output Gold.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is A wrong even though it runs with no error message?Show the answer

Ideas: the computer runs what is written, not what the programmer meant. Only the output shows the mistake.

steps.label: Your Notes: The Order of the Checks
steps.content:
Your Notes: The Order of the Checks

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

Order of the checks
With >=, check the highest number first: IF Score >= 80, then IF Score >= 50 inside the ELSE.
WHY 80 must come first
A score of 80 or more is also 50 or more. If the 50 check comes first, it is TRUE, the 80 check is skipped, and Gold is never output.
No error message
A program can run with no error message and still give the wrong output.

steps.label: Test Every Branch
steps.content:
Test Every Branch

The rule: a cinema ticket costs 40 baht for people aged 65 or older, and 100 baht for everyone else.

1  DECLARE Age : INTEGER
2  INPUT Age
3  IF Age > 65 THEN
4      OUTPUT 40
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT 100
7  ENDIF
Age typed inExpectedOutputResult
30100100Pass
704040Pass
6540100Fail
  • Test one value for each branch: 30 and 70 both pass.
  • Also test the number in the condition: 65 fails. Line 3 should use >=.
  • Write the expected output before you run the program.

WHY? A test passes only if the output matches the expected output. Without the expected output, a wrong answer can look fine.

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is "it gave an answer" not enough to say a program works?Show the answer

Ideas: the answer must match the rule. You need to know what it should be before you look.

steps.label: Your Notes: Test Every Branch
steps.content:
Your Notes: Test Every Branch

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the notes below. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

Test every branch
Use at least one value for each branch. Three outcomes need at least three values.
Test the number in the condition
For IF Age > 65, also type in 65. That shows a > and >= mix-up.
WHY write the expected output first
Then you can compare the real output with it and spot a mistake.

steps.label: Your Notes: Ready for Data Bridge
steps.content:
Your Notes: Ready for Data Bridge

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). You should have these six headings. Missing one? Go back to its slide and write it. You will use these notes in Data Bridge.

  • IF, THEN and ELSE: condition, selection and WHY only one branch runs.
  • Comparison Operators: the six operators and what they mean.
  • > and >=: the rule words and WHY to check the number in the condition.
  • Nested IF: three outcomes and how to trace it.
  • The Order of the Checks: WHY the highest number comes first.
  • Test Every Branch: one value for each branch, the number in the condition, and the expected output.
